# What is Poisson Nonnegative Matrix Factorization?

Let $X \in R_{+}^{n \times p}$ denote a matrix of observed counts $x_{ij}$. We assume $X_{ij} \sim Poi(\sum_k L_{ik}F_{jk})$.

Poisson NMF parameters include $L \in R_{+}^{n \times k}$
and $F \in R_{+}^{p \times k}$, and we seek values of L and F such that $X \approx LF^T$.


# Define likelihood-related functions

## 1. Incomplete data log likelihood

<!-- Eq 11.2 in Jordan chapter -->
Incomplete data log likelihood is defined as 
$$
\ell(\theta ; x) = \log p(x|\theta) = \log \sum_z p(x, z | \theta)
$$
In this simulation case, the incomplete log likelihood is
<!-- Notice I go from x to X matrix notation 
and i didn't specify L n k matrix etc k popped up out of nowhere
ADD note explaining its a summation of of Poisson PMF (X parametrized by L, F)-->

$$
\begin{align}
\ell(L,F; X) &= \log p(X| L,F) \\
&= \sum_{i} \sum_{j}[-\lambda_{ij} + X_{ij}\log(\lambda_{ij}) - \log(X_{ij}!)]
\end{align}
$$
given that $\lambda_{ij} = \sum_k L_{ik} F_{jk}$ for simpler notation.

## 2. Complete data log likelihood
<!-- Eq 11.1 in Jordan chapter -->
Complete data log likelihood is defined as below. In this case, theta is L and F.
$$
l_c(\theta; x,z) \triangleq \log p (x,z | \theta)
$$

Because the following assumption defines latent variable Z, access to X, L, F determines Z, without any randomness.

$$
Z_{ijk} \sim Poi(l_{ik} f_{jk}) \\
X_{ij} = \sum_k Z_{ijk}
$$

Thus complete data likelihood is equal to incomplete data likelihood within our model formulation.

$$
\begin{align}
l(L,F; X, Z) &= \log p(X, Z| L,F) \\
&= \log [p (Z | X, L, F) \times p(X | L, F)] \\
&= \sum_{i} \sum_{j}1 * [-\lambda_{ij} + X_{ij}\log(\lambda_{ij}) - \log(X_{ij}!)]
\end{align}
$$

## 3. Auxiliary function 
Also known as the lower bound for incomplete likelihood, auxiliary function for EM algorithm is defined as

$$
\mathcal{L}(q,\theta) = \sum_z q(z|x)\log \frac{p(x,z|\theta)}{q(z|x)}
$$

## E-step
Because of the way latent variable Z was defined, we can assume a multinomial distribution modelling z given x. Therefore, (also since multinomial parameter n is fixed to X) updating $q(z|x)$ is just a matter of choosing multinomial probabilities. Also, we know that the auxiliary function is maximized when $q^{(t+1)} (z|x) = p(z| x, \theta^t)$. Therefore, the E-step is

$$
\begin{align}
q^{(t+1)}(Z|X) &= p(z| x, \theta^t) \\
&= MN(n = X, p = \frac{l_{i:}f_{j:}}{\lambda_{ij}})
\end{align}
$$


## M-step
Once $q^{(t+1)}(Z|X)$ is updated, we want 

$$
\theta^{(t+1)} = \operatorname*{argmax}_\theta \mathcal{L}(q^{(t+1)}, \theta) 
$$

<!-- Refer to 11.13 for connection with expected complete log likelihood -->

$$
\begin{align}
\operatorname*{argmax}_\theta \mathcal{L}(q^{(t+1)}, \theta) &= \operatorname*{argmax}_\theta \langle \mathcal{l}_c(\theta ; x,z) \rangle_q \\
&= \operatorname*{argmax}_\theta \sum_z q(z|x) \log p (x,z|\theta) \\
&= \sum_z q(z|x) \operatorname*{argmax}_\theta \log p (x,z|\theta) \\
&= \operatorname*{argmax}_\theta \log p(\mathbb{E}[z] | \theta)
\end{align}
$$
Note $\mathbb{E}[z]$ is given from the multinomial distribution in E-step: $\mathbb{E}[z_{ij}] = X_{ij} \frac{l_{i:}f_{j:}}{\lambda_{ij}}$.
<!-- length k vectors-->

Going back to the latent variable representation $Z_{ijk} \sim Poi(l_{ik} f_{jk})$, $\mathbb{E}[z] \sim Poi(\theta)$ thus we can write  

<!-- Log Poisson PMF for X \sim Poi(\theta) -->

$$
p(\mathbb{E}[z] | \theta) = \sum_{ijk} (\mathbb{E}[z_{ijk}]\log(l_{ik}f_{jk}) - l_{ik}f_{jk} - \log \mathbb{E}[z_{ijk}]!)
$$


Taking partial derivative of log Poisson PMF with respect to $l_{ik}$ leads to 

$$
\begin{align}
\frac{\partial \ p(\mathbb{E}[z] | \theta)}{\partial \ l_{ik}} &= \sum_j (\frac{\mathbb{E}[z_{ijk}]}{l_{ik}} - f_{jk}) \\
\Rightarrow l_{ik}^\text{(new)} &= \sum_{j} \frac{\mathbb{E}[z_{ijk}]}{f_{jk}}
\end{align}
$$

Similarly, 

$$
f_{jk}^\text{(new)} = \sum_{i} \frac{\mathbb{E}[z_{ijk}]}{l_{ik}}
$$

# Implementation: EM

## Helper Function: E_step

```{r}
# Computes E_Z, which is a n x p x k matrix
E_step <- function(log_L, log_F, X){
  X_summary <-summary(X)
  x_val <- X_summary$x
  i <- X_summary$i
  j <- X_summary$j
  
  log_Lambda = compute_log_Lambda_mat(log_L, log_F, X)
  loglam_val <- log_Lambda@x
  
  # Compute W_ij = X_ij / Lambda_ij (Only for non-zeros)
  W_val <- exp(log(x_val) - loglam_val) 
  W <- sparseMatrix(i=i, j=j, x=W_val, dims=dim(X))
  
  # Fast sparse matrix multiplications in original space
  L <- exp(log_L)
  F <- exp(log_F)
  W_dot_F <- as.matrix(W %*% F)      # n x k
  Wt_dot_L <- as.matrix(t(W) %*% L)  # p x k
  
  # Back to log space
  logEz_sj = log_L + log(W_dot_F)  # Ez with j dimension summed, n x k
  logEz_si = log_F + log(Wt_dot_L) # Ez with i dimension summed, p x k
  
  # Return two squished slices of logEz
  return(list(logEz_sj = logEz_sj, logEz_si = logEz_si))
}

```

## Helper Function: M_step
```{r}
# Update log_L, log_F 
M_step <- function(log_L, log_F, E_res){
  # Prepare inputs
  logEz_sj = E_res$logEz_sj
  logEz_si = E_res$logEz_si
  
  # Update L first
  F <- exp(log_F)
  logF_sj = log(colSums(F)) # length k
  newlog_L = logEz_sj - rep(logF_sj, each = nrow(log_L))
  
  # Then update F
  L <- exp(log_L)
  logL_si = log(colSums(L)) # length k
  newlog_F = logEz_si - rep(logL_si, each = nrow(log_F))
  
  return(list(log_L=newlog_L, log_F=newlog_F))
}
```

## Helper Function: initialize_LF
Given generated X, output an initial guess of L, F

```{r}
library(fastTopics)
source(here("docs","code","initialize.R"))
source(here("docs","code","utils.R"))

initialize_LF <- function(X=X, K=3, shuffle=TRUE){
  # Estimate L, F: fasttopics
  ft = initialize(X=X, K=K)
  ftlog_L = ft$qg$qllog_norm
  ftlog_F = ft$qg$qflog_norm
  ft_res = compute_loglik(ftlog_L, ftlog_F, X)
  cat("fasttopics log-likelihood: ",ft_res[[1]])
  
  # Storage
  ft_ll = ft_res[1]
  ft_lamb = exp(ft_res[[2]])
  ft_L = exp(ftlog_L)
  ft_F = exp(ftlog_F)
  
  if (shuffle==TRUE){
    initlog_L = ftlog_L[sample(nrow(ftlog_L)),] # inject randomness since log_L overfit
  }
  else{
    initlog_L = ftlog_L
  }
  initlog_F = ftlog_F
  init_res = compute_loglik(initlog_L, initlog_F, X)
  
  # Storage
  init_ll = init_res[1]
  init_lamb = exp(init_res[[2]])
  init_L = exp(initlog_L)
  init_F = exp(initlog_F)
  
  # Need to format
  return(list(initlog_L=initlog_L,
             initlog_F=initlog_F,
             stor2 = list(ft_ll=ft_ll, ft_lamb=ft_lamb, 
                       ft_L=ft_L, ft_F=ft_F,
                       init_ll=init_ll, init_lamb=init_lamb, 
                       init_L=init_L, init_F=(init_F))))
}

```


## Top Level Helper Function: init_and_run_em
Main code chunk that initializes then runs EM over iterations.
Includes initialize_LF, E_step, M_step.

```{r}
init_and_run_em <- function(X=X, K=3, shuffle=TRUE,
                            experiment_gt = FALSE, data=data, # variables not used unless experiment_gt flag is TRUE
                            maxiter=20){
  if (experiment_gt==TRUE){init=list(initlog_L=log(data$L),initlog_F=log(data$F),stor2=list(ft_ll=NULL, ft_lamb=Matrix(), 
                       ft_L=Matrix(), ft_F=Matrix(),
                       init_ll=NULL, init_lamb=Matrix(), 
                       init_L=Matrix(), init_F=Matrix()))
  }
  else{init = initialize_LF(X=X, K=K, shuffle=shuffle)}
  

  # Initialize variables for loop 
  log_L = init$initlog_L
  log_F = init$initlog_F
  ll_list = rep(numeric(maxiter))

  for (niter in 1:maxiter){
    Ez_two = E_step(log_L, log_F, X)
    
    new = M_step(log_L, log_F, Ez_two)
    log_L = new$log_L
    log_F = new$log_F
  
    nres = compute_loglik(log_L, log_F, X)
    ll_list[niter] = nres[1]
    #cat("niter ",niter, "-------------", sprintf("LL: %.2f\n",  nres[1]))
  }
  
  # Storage
  final_lamb = exp(nres[[2]])
  final_L = exp(log_L)
  final_F = exp(log_F)
  
  stor3 = list(final_L = final_L, final_F = final_F, final_lamb = final_lamb, ll_list = ll_list)
  
  return(list(stor2=init$stor2,
              stor3=stor3))}
```


## Putting things together: full_EM_pipeline
Includes data generation code block, init_and_run_em, and visualization & metric code block.


<!-- Added seed and sparse X to main experiment. we are interested in a particular kind of count data $X$ such that there are K distinct hidden groups that we expect matrix factorization to reflect. Let's generate a small dataset with 3 distinct groups.-->


```{r}
source(here("docs","code","load_data.R"))
source(here("docs","code","utils.R"))
source(here("docs","code","initialize.R"))
library(pheatmap)
library(ggplot2)
library(Matrix)
library(pracma)

# "mix", "clear","news", "unif", "clear"
full_EM_pipeline <- function(data_type, w_matrix=NULL, experiment_gt=FALSE){
  set.seed(4) # else general_load gives slighly diff data each time
  # Data Generation
  data_type = data_type # "mix", "clear","news", "unif", "clear"
  data <- general_load(data_type=data_type, w_matrix = w_matrix)
  X = Matrix(data$X, sparse = TRUE)
  res = compute_loglik(log(data$L), log(data$F), X)
  
  # Storage
  gt_ll = res[1] # ground truth log likelihood
  gt_lamb = exp(res[[2]]) # mean(abs(X - exp(res[[2]]))) is Poisson noise floor
  gt_L = Matrix(data$L)
  gt_F = Matrix(data$F)
  stor1 = list(gt_ll=gt_ll, gt_lamb=gt_lamb, gt_L=gt_L, gt_F=gt_F)
  
  # --------------
  res_final = init_and_run_em(X=X, K=3, shuffle=TRUE, 
                              experiment_gt = experiment_gt, data=data,
                              maxiter=20)
  stor_all = c(stor1, res_final$stor2, res_final$stor3)
  # store_all = list(gt_ll, gt_lamb, gt_L, gt_F, # stor1
  #           ft_ll, ft_lamb, ft_L, ft_F, # stor2
  #           init_ll, init_lamb, init_L, init_F, # stor2
  #           ll_list, final_lamb final_L, final_F # stor3
  #           )
  
  # -------------
  source(here("docs","code","viz.R"))

  all_vals <- unlist(lapply(list(stor_all$gt_L,    stor_all$gt_F,
                                 stor_all$ft_L,    stor_all$ft_F,
                                 stor_all$init_L,  stor_all$init_F,
                                 stor_all$final_L, stor_all$final_F), 
                            as.numeric))
  print('\n -----')
  print("Correlation between k columns of EM L")
  print(cor(as.matrix(stor_all$final_L), method='pearson'))
  
  print("Correlation between k columns of EM F")
  print(cor(as.matrix(stor_all$final_F), method='pearson'))
  print('\n -----')
  
  
  global_breaks <- seq(min(all_vals, na.rm=TRUE), 
                       max(all_vals, na.rm=TRUE), 
                       length.out = 101)
  
  #Plots
  if (data_type == "news"){
    
  }
  else{
    try_run <- function(expr, label) {
   tryCatch(
    eval(substitute(expr), envir = parent.frame()),
    error = function(e) cat(sprintf("Skipped [%s]: %s\n", label, e$message)))}
    
    try_run(plot_lf(stor_all$gt_L,    stor_all$gt_F,    sprintf("%s - Ground Truth", data_type), global_breaks), "Ground Truth")
    try_run(plot_lf(stor_all$ft_L,    stor_all$ft_F,    "Fasttopics",  global_breaks),                           "Fasttopics LF")
    # try_run(plot_lf(stor_all$init_L,  stor_all$init_F,  "Initialized", global_breaks),                           "Initialized LF")
    try_run(plot_lf(stor_all$final_L, stor_all$final_F, "EM",          global_breaks),                           "EM LF")
    try_run(plot_em_ll(init_ll=stor_all$init_ll, ll_list=stor_all$ll_list, gt_ll=stor_all$gt_ll),                 "EM LL plot")

    ft_X     <- NA
    ft_lamb  <- NA
    
    try_run({
      ft_X    <- mean(abs(X - stor_all$ft_lamb))
      ft_lamb <- mean(abs(stor_all$gt_lamb - stor_all$ft_lamb))
    }, "Fasttopics MAE")
    
    try_run({
      poinoise <<- mean(abs(stor_all$gt_lamb - X))
      em_X     <<- mean(abs(X - stor_all$final_lamb))
      em_lamb  <<- mean(abs(stor_all$gt_lamb - stor_all$final_lamb))
    }, "EM MAE")
    
    try_run({
      met_res <- data.frame(
        Comparison = c("Poisson noise floor: true λ vs X",
                       "Fasttopics λ vs X", "Fasttopics λ vs true λ",
                       "EM λ vs X",         "EM λ vs true λ"),
        MAE = c(poinoise, ft_X, ft_lamb, em_X, em_lamb)
      )
      print(met_res, digits=2, row.names=FALSE)
    }, "Metrics table")
  }
  }
```


# A set of experiments

## Clear 3 groups case, perfect initialization
EM's results look very close to the ground truth, because of initialization (with the "answer"). 

EM is good at recovering Loadings, which have ground truth low variance. However, EM overestimates variance in Factors. True factors do not vary much within group, since its variance depends on normal noise with variance 1. 

Also, in this case EM seems to overfit to data X, rather than focusing on recovering true $LF^T$. It seems the term "overfitting to X" is interchangeable with MAE(algorithm-esimated $\Lambda = LF^T$, X) < MAE (True $\Lambda$, X) which is the Poisson noise floor.

EM log likelihood over iterations is well above the true $\Lambda$ log likelihood, reflecting the overfitting issue.

Pearson's correlation between L_k are more or less around -0.5, which is to be expected. We see similar correlation between F_k.
 
<!--Note spearman's corr(EM L_1, EM L_2) > corr(EM L_1, EM L_3), but I am not too interested in monotonicity by rank. EM loadings are clearly separated into three groups, so visually, difference between any two Loading columns are 2/3 of its rows. -->

```{r}
full_EM_pipeline("clear", experiment_gt=TRUE)
```

## Clear 3 groups case, shuffled fasttopics initialization

Since fasttopics $LF^T$ already overfits to X, it is not a good initialization for EM. If initialized with fasttopics, EM would get "stuck" and its results are more or less identical to fasttopics $LF^T$ (not shown in this document). Therefore, EM is initialized with fasttopics factors and row-permutated fasttopics loadings.

However, even with such initialization, visually EM loadings and factors are indistinguishable from fasttopics. Therefore, EM results reflect how fasttopics loadings are overexpressed and fasttopics factors are underexpressed.

Also in terms of MAE or final log likelihood, EM and fasttopics results are very similar.


```{r}
full_EM_pipeline("clear")
```

## Uniform groups case, shuffled fasttopics initialization
This case of simulated data has no underlying structure following k groups. All true loading and factor are randomly sampled between 0 and 1. This data generation is similar to fasttopics::simulate_count_data.

EM results overfit, and its MAE and log likelihood look very good.However, visually neither fasttopics or EM are doing well.


```{r}
full_EM_pipeline("unif")
```

## 3 groups with gamma prior case, shuffled fasttopics initialization
Very similar to uniform groups case: fasttopics and EM results are very similar visually and also in terms of MAE and log likelihood.

EM results did not overfit here, but EM is unable to recover underlying structure at all.

```{r}
# Define mixture weights for each L_k and F_k
# 21st mixture component (shape, rate) value is 1
l1 <- c(1, rep(0, 33)) # shape = 1e-16
l2 <- c(1, rep(0, 33)) # shape = 1e-16
l3 <- c(rep(0, 33), 1) # shape = 1000
f1 <- c(1, rep(0, 33)) # shape = 1e-16
f2 <- c(rep(0, 33), 1) # shape = 1000
f3 <- c(rep(0, 33), 1) # shape = 1000
# Weights will be normalized by column inside visualize_mixtures or generate_synthetic
# First visualize each mixture
cusw <- cbind(l1,l2,l3,f1,f2,f3)
visualize_mixtures(cusw)

full_EM_pipeline("mix", w_matrix=cusw)
```

# Questions for the future

While not shown in the current rmarkdown version, cosine similarity between vectors doesn't seem to be a good metric conveying information about the quality of estimated $l_k$, since it cannot differentiate between true $l_k$ or $f_k$ anyways. I hoped cosine similarity between true vectors would be close to zero, so that true vs. estimated vectors would give insight to the degree of different information carried by K estimated vectors.

S. Amari, Information geometry of the EM and em algorithms for neural networks (1995) gives a geometric view of the EM algorithm. I'm interested in how the overfitted PMF solution would fit into this view.

$\log p(x, z| \theta) $ is the complete log likelihood, can be obtained if latent Z was observed. $Z= LF^T$  in my case is the clean data where the real world data was pulled from with $X = Poi (Z)$. However, Z cannot be observed, so we are forced to work with incomplete log likelihood, equal to marginalized complete log-likelihood.
$$ 
\begin{align}
\log p(x|\theta) &= log \sum_z p(x,z | \theta) \\
&= l(\theta ; x) \text{<-  log likelihood}
\end{align}
$$

Given that Z is not observed, complete log likelihood $\log p(x, z| \theta)$ is a random quantity. To remove the randomness in complete log likelihood, we can average over z drawn from a estimated distribution $q(z|x,\theta). Then we can define the expected complete log likelihood as
$$
\langle l(\theta ; x, z) \rangle _q = \sum_z q (z | x,\theta) \log p (x,z | \theta)
$$
Note posterior probability of the latent variable z $p(z| x, \theta^{(t)})$ is the optimal $q^{(t+1)}(z|x)$ with 

Averaging over z removes stochasticity associated with z, making expected complete log likelihood no longer a random variable but a deterministic function over $\theta$. This ensures auxiliary function $L(q, \theta^{t})$ (also the lower bound on log likelihood) becomes equal to log likelihood.
